args.text: [lane-vole] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: if a service moves to a new server, users keep being sent to the old one, causing outages or errors. (2) Slow recovery and failover: when you change records to route around a fault, the change takes longer to reach users. (3) Longer exposure to bad data: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache for longer before it expires, so more people are affected.

[lane-vole] Idempotent retries matter because a request that can be repeated safely, with the same result as running it once, lets a client try again after a timeout without fear of doing the work twice. Without that guarantee, a retry could cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

[lane-vole] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) It is time-ordered, so inserts stay mostly sequential and indexes behave well, but it exposes the creation time to anyone who sees the key. (2) It is 16 bytes, larger than a 4 or 8 byte integer, so indexes and foreign keys take more space and memory, and ordering within the same millisecond depends on the implementation.

[lane-vole] A write-ahead log is a record of each change that a database writes to durable storage before it alters the main data files. If the system crashes, it can replay the log to recover committed work and discard unfinished changes, which keeps the data consistent.

[lane-vole] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Comparable results: a newer client may change defaults, retries or performance, so unpinned runs could differ for reasons unrelated to the system under test. (2) Reproducibility: others can rerun the same set-up later and get consistent figures, and any change in results can be traced to a deliberate update.

[lane-vole] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal to the senders that it is filling up faster than the receivers can empty it. The senders then slow down, wait or reject new work, which stops the queue growing without limit and exhausting memory.

[lane-vole] Two ways a cron job (a scheduled task) can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two machines, for example after scaling out or a failover, so both fire at once; (2) a slow run is still going when the next one starts, so the runs overlap. One guard: take a lock before working, such as a lock file or a database lock with an expiry, and exit at once if another run holds it.

[lane-vole] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, saying that the item was removed and when. In a replicated store it stops a copy that missed the deletion from sending the old value back to the others, which would bring the item back to life. Tombstones are only cleared after a grace period, once every copy has seen them. How long that period should be is unknown here.

[lane-vole] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs, so a simple re-run gives a different result. (2) The failure depends on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or the machine used, and it often goes away when the test is run alone. A truly failing test fails every time for the same reason.

[lane-vole] A lease-based lock gives a worker the lock for a set time, after which it expires. Clock skew means two machines disagree about what time it is. If the lock holder's clock runs slow, it believes its lease is still valid after the server has already expired it and given the lock to someone else. Then two workers act at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. A common fix is a fencing token, a rising number that the protected resource checks, so stale holders are rejected.
